title: Multiplying and dividing in polar form

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the product's arc made of z's arc and w's arc stacked end to end, and its length r × s, when you drag w's tip round and out.
interactive.title: Turn and stretch
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the complex plane from the earlier lessons, real across and j up. Two arrows run from 0: z, of length r at angle θ, and w, of length s at angle φ, each with its angle drawn as an arc from the positive real axis and its length labelled. You can drag w's tip. A third arrow, drawn bold, is the product z × w. Its arc is z's arc with w's arc laid on the end of it, so its angle is θ + φ, and its length is labelled r × s. That is because multiplying by w does to z what it does to 1, the arrow of length 1 at 0°: it turns it through w's angle and stretches it s times, a shrink if s is less than 1. A divide switch shows z ÷ w instead: w's arc is taken away from the end of z's arc, so the angle is θ − φ, and the length is r ÷ s. A × j button sets w to 1∠90°, the quarter turn from the first lesson, so the product is z turned a quarter turn with its length unchanged. When the angle goes past half a turn, a whole-turn arc of 360° shows the same arrow named with an angle in the usual range. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? replays the arcs and lengths for it.
interactive.ignores: The tip of w snaps to half steps of length, from 0.5 to 3, and 10° steps of angle, so the sums can be followed, but lengths and angles can be any numbers, and the rules work the same for them. Lengths and angles are rounded to two decimal places, so a check by going back to parts can be out in the last place. Angles are in degrees; calculators and college texts also use radians, where 180° is π, and the rules are the same. 0 has length 0 and no angle, so multiplying by 0 gives 0, and dividing by 0 has no answer.

explain.text:
In polar form, multiplying is a turn and a stretch you can read straight off: multiply the lengths and add the angles.[^3] Dividing undoes it: divide the lengths and take the angles away.[^4] That is why multiplying and dividing are easiest in polar form, while adding and taking away are easiest in parts.[^5]

Remember from the multiplying lesson: whatever turn and stretch takes 1 to w also takes any arrow z to z × w. The arrow 1 has length 1 and angle 0°, and 1 × w is w itself. So if w is s∠φ, multiplying by w takes 1 to an arrow s long at angle φ: it turns 1 through φ and stretches it s times, which is a shrink when s is less than 1. It does exactly the same to z = r∠θ: it turns through φ to angle θ + φ, and its length becomes r × s. On the picture, the product's arc is z's arc with w's arc laid on the end of it, and its length is r × s. So 2∠30° × 3∠40° is 2 × 3 = 6 long at 30° + 40° = 70°: 6∠70°. Times j is the plainest case. j is 1∠90°, so it adds 90° and stretches by 1, which is no stretch at all: a pure quarter turn anticlockwise, as in the first lesson.[^1] Check the rule against the parts. (3 + j4)(4 + j3) multiplied out is 12 + j9 + j16 + j × j × 12 = 12 − 12 + j25 = j25. In polar form 3 + j4 is 5∠53.13° and 4 + j3 is 5∠36.87°, so the product is 5 × 5 = 25 long at 53.13° + 36.87° = 90°: 25∠90°, which is j25. Adding the lengths would give 10, but j25 is 25 long, so the lengths multiply.

Dividing asks which number, multiplied by w, gives z. Multiplying by w adds φ to the angle and multiplies the length by s, so the answer must do the opposite: angle θ − φ and length r ÷ s. So 6∠70° ÷ 3∠40° = 2∠30°, and multiplying back gives 6∠70° again. Take the bottom's angle away from the top's, not the other way round: 12∠80° ÷ 4∠30° is 3∠50°, and 3∠−50° is a different arrow. Check against the conjugate lesson: 10 ÷ (3 + j4) came to 1.2 − j1.6, and in polar form 10∠0° ÷ 5∠53.13° = 2∠−53.13°, whose parts are 2 cos(−53.13°) = 1.2 across and 2 sin(−53.13°) = −1.6 up, the same number. Dividing by j = 1∠90° takes 90° away, a quarter turn back, which is why 1 ÷ j came to −j in that lesson: 1∠−90°.

Added angles can go past half a turn: 5∠150° × 2∠60° = 10∠210°. Taking away 360°, a whole turn, leaves the arrow where it is, so it is also 10∠−150°, back in the usual range of more than −180° and up to 180°.[^2] Multiplying the lengths and adding the angles is the rule for multiplying, not for adding. To add, go back to parts: 1∠0° + 1∠90° is 1 + j1, which is 1.41∠45°, not 2∠90°. Engineering maths texts also write r∠θ as re^(jθ), the same arrow, with θ in radians.[^6][^7] **To multiply in polar form, multiply the lengths and add the angles; to divide, divide the lengths and take the angles away.[^3][^4]**

analogy.text: Feed a supply through two transformers in turn. If the first steps the voltage down 2 to 1 and the second 5 to 1, the pair steps it down 10 to 1: the ratios multiply, they do not add. From your trade rather than from this lesson's sources: a transformer whose windings are wired star on one side and delta on the other also shifts the phase, and two in a row shift it by the sum of their shifts. Sizes multiply and angles add, as with r∠θ × s∠φ.
analogy.breaks: A real transformer's ratio holds only approximately under load, since its windings drop some voltage, and its phase shift is set by how its windings are connected, so it cannot take any angle you like. The complex numbers here multiply exactly, at any length and any angle.

practice.text:
- Put each number into polar form, as in the last lesson: sketch it, find the length with Pythagoras and the angle with tan⁻¹, and check the quarter.
- To multiply: multiply the lengths and add the angles.
- To divide: divide the top's length by the bottom's, and take the bottom's angle away from the top's.
- Bring the angle into the usual range: if it is more than 180°, take 360° away; if it is −180° or less, add 360°.
- Check by going back to parts with r cos θ and r sin θ, or by multiplying back.

**Rule of thumb:** Add and take away in parts; multiply and divide in polar form.[^5]

**Rule of thumb:** Times j adds 90° and dividing by j takes 90° away. Neither changes the length.

**Worked example:** (6 + j8) ÷ (1 + j1). The top is √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 long at tan⁻¹(8 ÷ 6) = 53.13°, so it is 10∠53.13°. The bottom is √2 = 1.414 long at 45°, so it is 1.414∠45°. Divide the lengths: 10 ÷ 1.414 = 7.07. Take the angles away: 53.13° − 45° = 8.13°. So the answer is 7.07∠8.13°. Check by going back: 7.07 cos 8.13° = 7 and 7.07 sin 8.13° = 1, so it is 7 + j1. The conjugate agrees: (6 + j8)(1 − j1) = 14 + j2, and the bottom (1 + j1)(1 − j1) = 2, so the answer is 7 + j1.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the lengths. 5∠53.13° × 5∠36.87° is 25∠90°, not 10∠90°.
- Multiplying the angles. The turns stack end to end, so the angles add: 4∠25° × 2∠50° is 8∠75°.
- Taking the angles away in the wrong order. 12∠80° ÷ 4∠30° is 3∠50°, not 3∠−50°.
- Adding in polar form. 1∠0° + 1∠90° is 1 + j1 = 1.41∠45°, not 2∠90°. Go back to parts to add.
- Leaving an angle such as 210° out of the usual range. Take 360° away: −150°.
